opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they're quite different things. In the physical world, you're dealing with an environment that pushes back on you. You take an action, and something happens, and you don't fully know what that will be. You have to make predictions about what will happen, and then you get to see whether you were right. That's the essence of learning from experience. There's ground truth that arrives over time, and you can learn from it.

Mathematics is more computational. It's more like planning. You have the rules, they're given to you, and the problem is one of search: working through the consequences until you find a proof or an answer. There's no surprise coming from an external world. In that sense it's closer to something like playing Go, where the dynamics are known and you just have to compute well.

Now, can you have a goal in solving a math problem? Yes, you can. You can say the goal is to find a proof, and you can get a reward when you find one. That's a legitimate goal, and it's different from what large language models are fundamentally doing, which is predicting the next token. Predicting the next token isn't a goal about the world. It doesn't change anything; it's just mimicking what people said.

So when people point to LLMs doing well on math, I'd say that's the more tractable case, because it's a closed, well-defined domain. Modeling the physical world is the harder and more important problem. It requires an agent that acts, predicts what will actually happen, not what a person would say, and learns from the consequences. That's what I think intelligence really is, and that's where I think the LLM approach falls short.

r001.rationale: It says physical-world learning comes from experience: actions have uncertain outcomes, and the agent observes whether its predictions were right over time.

r002.rationale: It describes mathematics as planning with given rules, searching through their consequences to find a proof or answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they're quite different kinds of things, and the difference matters a lot.

When a large language model solves a math problem, there's really no goal in the sense I mean the word. The system is predicting what a person would say next, and in mathematics, what a person would say next happens to coincide with the right answer much of the time. There's no consequence to the system for getting it wrong. Nothing in the world pushes back. The ground truth is what the people in the training data wrote down. So I'd say it's not a goal, it's an imitation of goal-directed behavior. A goal, to me, means there's something you're trying to make happen, you can tell whether it happened, and you're surprised and you change when it doesn't.

Modeling the physical world is a fundamentally different proposition because the world is the thing that tells you whether you're right. You take an action, you make a prediction about what you'll see, and then you see something. That's the ground truth, and it's available continually, for every moment of experience, without anybody labeling it. That's what I mean by a world model. It's a prediction of consequences, of what will happen if I do this, and it's checked against what actually happens.

Now, people will say the language model has a world model too, because it can talk about the world sensibly. But it's a model of what people say about the world, not a model of the world. Those are correlated, but they come apart as soon as you're in a situation nobody has written about, or as soon as the question is about the consequences of your own actions in a particular situation, rather than about what the typical text says.

So the distinction I'd draw is about where the error signal comes from. In the math case, the signal is agreement with people. In the world modeling case, the signal is agreement with the world. And I think only the second one leads to real intelligence, because only the second one lets the system keep learning after you stop supervising it. That's the thing I care about: continual learning from experience, where the agent has goals, acts, and is corrected by reality rather than by us.

r001.rationale: The response says a world model predicts what will happen after an action and checks that prediction against what actually happens, making physical consequences an empirical learning signal.

r002.rationale: The response describes solving math as imitating what people would say, but does not characterize deriving consequences from mathematical assumptions as planning.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish a goal from a model. Solving a mathematical problem is a goal: there’s some answer you’re trying to find, and you can judge whether you’ve succeeded. Modeling the physical world is about predicting what will happen, perhaps as a consequence of different actions. That model can help you achieve a goal, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell you what goal to pursue.

And an LLM can be involved in either activity. The question is what it learns from. If it produces a mathematical answer, does it get feedback about whether the answer is correct, and does that feedback change its future behavior? If it predicts something about the world, does it observe what actually happens and improve its predictions?

The distinction I care about is whether the system is continually learning from the consequences of its behavior. You can describe a task in language, and you can produce something that looks like a solution in language. But that’s different from having an ongoing process of trying things, discovering where your expectations were wrong, and learning to do better.

r001.rationale: It says a world model should be checked against what actually happens and improved, and emphasizes learning from consequences of behavior.

r002.rationale: It contrasts finding a mathematical answer with predicting the world, but does not characterize deriving consequences from mathematical assumptions as planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish having a goal from having a model. A goal tells you which outcomes you prefer. A model tells you what you expect to happen. Those are different things, and you can have either one without the other.

If you give an LLM a mathematical problem, you’ve specified a task, but that doesn’t by itself tell us in what sense the system has adopted a goal. Is it selecting actions based on their consequences for getting the answer right? Or is it producing text that resembles solutions? Those might look similar in a particular example, but they’re different accounts of what the system is doing.

And modeling the physical world isn’t necessarily goal-directed either. You could just predict the next observation. The connection comes when an agent uses its model to predict the consequences of its actions, and then chooses actions that help it achieve a goal. So I wouldn’t draw the fundamental distinction between mathematics and the physical world. I’d draw it between prediction and control—between anticipating what will happen and acting to make something happen.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can predict physical observations and action consequences, but does not state that those consequences must be learned empirically.

r002.rationale: It discusses mathematical problems and choosing actions to achieve goals, but does not characterize deriving consequences from mathematical assumptions as planning.
